ron: A forty-six-year-old just made his debut in Italy's third division. His name is Ronaldinho. Yes, that one.
The only player ever to win the World Cup, the Copa América, the Confederations Cup, the Champions League, the Copa Libertadores and the Ballon d'Or. I once won a meat raffle.

It started young. At eight they called him Ronaldinho, little Ronaldo, because he was the smallest boy on the pitch. At thirteen he scored all twenty-three goals in a twenty-three-nil win. His team-mates came for the oranges.

Then the World Cup. Two thousand and two, Brazil against England. A free-kick from forty yards curled past David Seaman into the top corner. Seven minutes later, sent off. Genius, then a red card. Relatable.
Barcelona, two thousand and five: Ballon d'Or. Real Madrid's own fans stood and applauded him at the Bernabéu. Voluntarily. The first Barça player to get that since Maradona.
So what happened? Football moved on. His last club before Ravenna was Fluminense in two thousand and fifteen. Nine games. He retired in two thousand and eighteen.

So why is a forty-six-year-old legend at Ravenna? They are in Serie C, Italy's third division. Their owner, Ignazio Cipriani, announced it at the World Cup in June. Subtle. Ronaldinho is a player and a minority shareholder, though some reports said it was mostly marketing. He says he wants a three hundredth career goal.
And on Sunday, against Forlì, he walked out in white. Flares. Smoke. Serie C glamour. Nineteenth minute: a corner. Saved. Ravenna won two-nil.
Forty-six, one corner kick, still the most famous man in Serie C. Your uncle from Sunday league has no more excuses.
mud: A winger who cost up to a hundred million euros was asked what that feels like. His answer: a dump truck.
Meet Mykhailo Mudryk. Shakhtar Donetsk to Chelsea, January twenty twenty-three. Seventy million euros up front, up to a hundred with add-ons. The most expensive Ukrainian footballer ever.
But his real trademark is pace. The interviewer says that in twenty twenty-two he was officially the fastest player in the Champions League.
Then the Premier League. Reports put his Chelsea salary at four hundred thousand pounds a month.
Gross. As in, before tax. So how big is the tax?
Dinner with Messi and Ronaldo, anyone?
These days: a long anti-doping case ended with all charges dropped in July. Twenty months without a competitive match. In September he joined Tottenham on loan, reunited with Roberto De Zerbi.
A hundred-million price tag. Forty-five percent tax. Thirty-seven point four kilometres an hour. He can outrun everything except the taxman.

por: A hundred and forty-six goals. Two hundred and thirty-four caps. Both world records. And on the fifth of November, Cristiano Ronaldo handed Portugal's number seven shirt back.
Twenty-three years. Captain of the Euro two thousand and sixteen winners.
So why now? Reports say it followed a dispute with coach Jorge Jesus over selection plans. Reported, not confirmed.
He is not quitting football. He carries on at club level.
Portugal's only question left: who wears seven next? And good luck to them with the comments section.
